P1.evidence: No application or setter notes were referenced at any point; the rep in fact asked 'what's your work again, I don't know if we talked about work', which suggests nothing was reviewed beforehand. The four-part frame was delivered, compressed but complete: 'I want to kind of figure out where we're at, where we're trying to get to, what's missing, and then we can maybe map out a coaching program from there.' No frame agreement was taken — he went straight from the frame into the open question with no 'does that work?' The open question itself ran: 'what do you feel we can potentially help you with? Give me a rundown.'

P2.evidence: Coverage is good. Age asked at 00:09:36, height and weight at 00:15:18. Work established and then corrected when the rep assumed movement — 'so work, you're moving around a lot' drew 'at my work, there's actually quite a lot of sitting. I'm in an office most of the time,' which is exactly what the check is for. The injury question was asked plainly — 'Any, like, current injuries or health conditions or anything like that?' — and produced hypermobility, the seven-foot scaffold fall, the displaced vertebra, uneven hips and the back locking, with durations. Training frequency pinned to actuals: 'How many times a week are you actually working out right now?' Diet asked and covered. P2c is partial because hereditary conditions were never asked for — the family heart attacks and both parents' conditions were volunteered — and the mental health disclosure came unprompted at the very end of discovery. Sleep and energy were never asked about, which is a notable gap given daily headaches and depressive and manic episodes. The larger issue is not coverage but what followed: the rep collected a serious clinical picture and asked not one follow-up question about any part of it.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals work in this batch. Magic wand run cleanly: 'if I had a magic wand, and we could create the perfect physique and perfect fitness situation, like, what would that look like for you?' The something-you-can't-do check is genuinely satisfied — Sundance, lifting logs in ceremony, keeping pace with his roommate hiking in August, summits. Bridge asked twice, including 'why else is this important for you now, all of a sudden? Because, I mean, you've been just kind of coasting for so many years, right?' P3e run verbatim in spirit: 'What else would that do for you if you looked good and felt good in your body? What else would that do?' P3g reached without prompting to his son, to being alive for grandchildren, to mortality and to the elders in ceremony he does not want to become. P3f is partial because the son arrived volunteered rather than asked for. P3h is partial — 'Sounds like you're just looking for a bit of a system, is that what I'm understanding?' reflects the surface want back, not the deep why, and the deep why on this call was self-worth.

P4.evidence: All six ran. 'So what have we tried before to solve all this?' produced the honest answer — 'Not a lot. Like I've just been living this way for years' — plus the bodybuilder friend, the gifted mobility programme from the Australian couple, and repeatedly asking friends for help. Why it did not stick was asked directly on the diet: 'Why do you think you haven't had consistency with that?' The prospect named the gap himself and precisely: 'It's just not having somebody there with me. That's been the most difficult part. It really has,' and 'Doing it solo hasn't worked for me. It just hasn't.' P4f ran as the Einstein line plus the janitor-versus-plumber vehicle analogy — 'you can work as hard as you want as a janitor, it's just not happening' — which is a strong variant of the scripted move, though the rep also wrapped it in 'you're trying to fix a fat person problem from a fat person mindset', which the prospect later said he registered.

P5.evidence: The two-year question ran and produced the strongest material on the call: 'what happens if we don't actually make the change, man?' drew bedridden, depressed, back seizing, chronic headaches, and 'I don't want to die from a heart attack. Men in my family die from heart attacks, dude.' The line in the sand ran: 'So you're ready to draw a line in the sand then, or how are you feeling?' / 'That's pretty much where I'm at.' The middle of the phase is missing — the settle-for test and the why-not follow-up were never asked, so the consequence was surfaced but never pressed into a commitment.

P6.evidence: P6b ran cleanly and, importantly, before the price: 'Provided we can figure out the finances, because I know that was the biggest thing, are you truly committed to showing up fully and doing the work to actually make this transformation?' answered 'Yeah, I am. I've reached a point in my life where it's time.' P6c is a hit on sequencing — the yes was obtained at 01:02:12 and the price quoted at 01:02:40, in the right order. P6a is partial: the scripted belief question was not asked, but a one-to-ten rating with a gap-closing follow-up did equivalent work — 'Everything we talked about, 1-10... Where would you say this is at?' produced 'I'd say a solid 8', and 'what's the last two points to get you to a full 10?' isolated the two real blockers, money and self-doubt.

P11.evidence: The close was attempted and the prospect was disqualified on affordability, so payment and onboarding were never reachable. No payment was collected, no onboarding call booked and no agreement sent.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in this batch and close to the script. Isolation ran twice and well: 'If I handed you a duffel bag full of cash that covered the cost of the investment, would you do it?' then pushing past 'Sure, probably' with 'Okay, probably or definitely?', and again with 'is it more uncertainty on the investment or is we just don't have the investment?' The permission question ran almost verbatim: 'are you open to having an open and honest conversation about where you're at financially?' Then the financial picture, in order — income, monthly expenses, surplus ('So that leaves us with $500 a month, something like that?'), credit availability ('what do we actually have available on credit?' / 'I have nothing available. And they're completely maxed'), card limits, savings and investments, and cash on hand ('How much do you actually have in the [chequing] account right now?'). Only the crypto and stocks prompt was folded into the savings question rather than asked separately. The play was run properly and produced an honest answer, and the rep correctly did not push a close the prospect could not fund.

Self-doubt was named explicitly at 00:55:19 and the rep asked for more — 'tell me more about the doubt in your own self' — which was the right move. The reframe that followed carried the substance of the scripted BRIDGE: 'you'll never know with 100% complete certainty what anything in life will be like... there's really two types of people' proactive versus reactive. None of the actual scripted moves ran — no 'would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty?', no pleasure-versus-pain question, no plane analogy, no burned-before frame, no 'how will you know if you never actually try?' It did land: he re-committed at 01:02:25.

'I think I do need to sleep on it' arrived at 01:03:38. The rep did not run OA and instead re-routed straight to the money isolation, which was the correct diagnosis — the real blocker was cash, not deliberation, and the duffel-bag question proved it inside thirty seconds. Scored partial rather than miss because the redirection was deliberate and correct, but none of the OA moves themselves ran.

The script has no exit ramp for a prospect who genuinely cannot afford the programme. OC is built on the assumption that capacity exists somewhere and needs surfacing — cash, cards, credit, investments. Here every one of those came back empty and honestly: maxed cards, no savings, about $100 in the account, roughly $500 a month spare. At that point the rep had nothing scripted to do, and improvised a $1,000 self-serve product that is not one of the two sanctioned tiers. This is a genuine gap in the playbook and a predictable one — it will recur — and it deserves a sanctioned answer rather than live invention. Proposed label: affordability_floor_reached.

A trust and fit objection was raised and completely ignored: 'I've never met Trevor. I don't know his energy. Are we actually gonna jive as people? Like, if I don't like the guy, I'm not gonna be able to work with him.' There is no scripted play for it and the rep gave no response whatsoever, moving on to the commitment question. For a six-month one-to-one offer sold by someone other than the coach, this is a foreseeable objection with an easy answer, and the script has none.

notes: Discovery, root cause and the money play were the best-executed in this batch, and the rep deserves credit for running the financial picture honestly and then declining to push a close the prospect could not fund. Two things need correcting. First, the clinical follow-up: he asked the injury question, received hypermobility with unstable knees, a displaced vertebra from a seven-foot fall, daily crippling pain and manic and depressive episodes, and asked nothing further about any of it — then encouraged immediate kettlebell conditioning ahead of a four-day fast-and-dance ceremony nine days out. Second, the improvised $1,000 product. Both stem from the same underlying gap: when the script runs out, this rep invents, and here he invented in a direction with real safety and pricing exposure. Also coach the un-answered question about whether he and Trevor would get on.
